\begin{center}
{\textbf{A counterexample to the cubic implication for hyperfields}}
\end{center}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Abstract.}
In a field, $x+y+z=0$ implies $x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz=0$.  We show that the
analogous implication for hyperfields,
\[
 0\in x\bp y\bp z
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 0\in x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz),
\]
fails in general, although it holds in every quotient $F/G$ of a field
by a multiplicative subgroup.  The counterexample is a hyperfield
attached, following Prenowitz and Connes--Consani, to an infinite
cyclic projective plane; the plane is built from a perfect difference
set in $\Z$ by an explicit variant of Hall's extension argument.  All
hyperfield axioms are verified directly, so the paper is
self-contained.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

\paragraph{Conventions.}
A \emph{hyperoperation} on a set $\Hh$ is a map $\bp$ assigning to each
pair $(a,b)$ a nonempty subset $a\bp b\subseteq\Hh$.  It is extended to
subsets by the union convention
\begin{equation}\label{eq:union}
 A\bp B=\bigcup_{a\in A,\ b\in B}(a\bp b),
\end{equation}
an element being identified with its singleton.  Thus
$x\bp y\bp z$ means $(x\bp y)\bp z=\bigcup_{s\in x\bp y}(s\bp z)$, and
in an expression such as $(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)$ each occurrence is a
separate summand; this is the reading intended in the question below.
In a hyperfield (Definition~\ref{def:hyperfield}) the hyperaddition is
associative, and then iterated sums do not depend on the bracketing
(Remark~\ref{rem:iterated}).

\paragraph{The question.}
In a field, $x+y+z=0$ implies $x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz=0$, because of the
polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic}
 x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz=(x+y+z)(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx).
\end{equation}
A \emph{hyperfield} is, roughly, a field whose addition is multivalued;
the precise definition is recalled in Section~\ref{sec:hyperfields}.
The question asks whether the implication survives in that generality.

\begin{question}
Let $\Hh$ be a hyperfield with hyperaddition $\bp$, and let
$x,y,z\in\Hh$ satisfy $0\in x\bp y\bp z$.  Does it follow that
\[
 0\in x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\,?
\]
\end{question}

\noindent
Here $x^3$ is the multiplicative cube and $-xyz$ the additive inverse
(the \emph{negative}) of the product $xyz$.  We call the implication
asked about the \emph{cubic implication}.  The answer is no.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
There exist a countably infinite commutative hyperfield $\Hh$ and
elements $x,y,z\in\Hh$ such that $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ but
\[
 0\notin x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz).
\]
\end{theorem}

\paragraph{Why a counterexample must be a non-quotient hyperfield.}
The most familiar hyperfields are Krasner's quotients $F/G$ of a field
$F$ by a subgroup $G$ of its multiplicative group
[Kr83] (recalled in Example~\ref{ex:quotient}).  In every such hyperfield the cubic
implication \emph{does} hold (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient}): the
hypothesis $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ provides representatives $u,v,w\in F$
with $u+v+w=0$, and the field identity~\eqref{eq:cubic} for $u,v,w$
produces the required $0$.  Consequently a counterexample has to be a
hyperfield that is not a quotient of a field, so its hyperfield axioms
cannot be inherited from a field; we verify them directly in
Section~\ref{sec:hyperfield}, which is the main technical work of the
paper.

\paragraph{Strategy.}
The construction follows the geometric recipe of Prenowitz~[Pr43] and
Connes--Consani~[CC11, \S3].  Let $P$ be the point set of a projective
plane, in the weak sense that any two distinct points lie on exactly one
line and any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point, and write
$L(a,b)$ for the line through two distinct points $a,b$; three points
are \emph{collinear} if one line contains them and \emph{noncollinear}
otherwise, and the \emph{sides} of a noncollinear triple (a
\emph{triangle}) $a,b,c$ are the three lines $L(a,b),L(a,c),L(b,c)$.
On $\Hh=P\cup\{0\}$ define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a\bp b&=L(a,b)\setminus\{a,b\} &&(a,b\in P,\ a\neq b),\\
 a\bp a&=\{0,a\} &&(a\in P),\\
 0\bp a&=a\bp0=\{a\} &&(a\in\Hh)
 \end{aligned}
\]
(this is~\eqref{eq:addition} below).  If, in addition, every line is
infinite, $P$ is an abelian group, and
multiplication by every element of $P$ maps lines to lines, then $\Hh$
with this hyperaddition and the group multiplication is a commutative
hyperfield; this is proved for our plane in
Proposition~\ref{prop:hyperfield} by an argument that uses only these
properties (compare [CC11, Propositions~3.1 and~3.5], where four points
per line suffice).  Three features of this hyperfield drive the
counterexample.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Every element is its own negative: $0\in a\bp b$ if and only
if $a=b$.  Hence $-xyz=xyz$, and for subsets $A,B\subseteq\Hh$ one has
$0\in A\bp B$ if and only if $A\cap B\neq\varnothing$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:zero}).
\item[(b)] If $a,b,c$ are distinct points on a common line $L$, then
$a\bp b\bp c=L\cup\{0\}$; in particular $0\in a\bp b\bp c$.
\item[(c)] If $a,b,c$ are noncollinear, then
$a\bp b\bp c=P\setminus\bigl(L(a,b)\cup L(a,c)\cup L(b,c)\bigr)$ is
the complement of the three sides of the triangle $a,b,c$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}); in particular $0\notin a\bp b\bp c$.
\end{enumerate}
Now let $x,y,z$ be distinct collinear points, so that $0\in x\bp y\bp z$
by~(b), and put $q=xyz=-xyz$.  The defining rules give
$q\bp q\bp q=\{0,q\}\bp q=\{q\}\cup\{0,q\}=\{0,q\}$, so by associativity
the six-term sum of the question equals $S\bp\{0,q\}$ with
$S=x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3$, and by~(a) it contains $0$ if and only if $S$
meets $\{0,q\}$.  Suppose the cubes $x^3,y^3,z^3$ are noncollinear.
Then (c) says that $0\notin S$ and that $q\in S$ exactly when $q$ lies
on none of the sides of the triangle $x^3,y^3,z^3$.  The question has
thus become one of pure incidence geometry: the cubic implication fails
for $x,y,z$ precisely when the product $q=xyz$ lies on a side of the
``cube triangle''.  So we need a plane whose points form a group acting
by collineations, containing three collinear points whose cubes are
noncollinear and whose product lies on a side of the cube triangle.

\paragraph{Cyclic planes.}
Let $P=\{t^j:j\in\Z\}$ be an infinite cyclic group and let
$D\subseteq\Z$ be a \emph{perfect difference set}: every nonzero
integer has exactly one representation $d-e$ with $d,e\in D$.  The sets
$L_k=\{t^{k+d}:d\in D\}$, $k\in\Z$, are then the lines of a projective
plane on $P$, and multiplication by $t^r$ carries $L_k$ to $L_{k+r}$
(Section~\ref{sec:plane}).  This is the classical correspondence between
cyclic planes and difference sets, due to Singer~[Si38] for finite
planes and to Hall~[Ha47] for the group $\Z$.  Choose
\[
 x=1,\qquad y=t,\qquad z=t^3,\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
 x^3=1,\quad y^3=t^3,\quad z^3=t^9,\quad q=xyz=t^4.
\]
The requirements become conditions on $D$: if $0,1,3\in D$ then $x,y,z$
lie on $L_0$; if $20,24,29\in D$ then $1$, $q=t^4$ and $t^9$ lie on
$L_{-20}$, which is therefore the side $L(1,t^9)$ of the cube triangle;
and the uniqueness of differences then forces $23\notin D$ (because
$23-20=3-0$), so that $t^3\notin L_{-20}$ and the cubes are
noncollinear.  Hall proved that every finite set of integers with
pairwise distinct differences is contained in a perfect difference set
of $\Z$ [Ha47, Theorem~3.1].  Section~\ref{sec:diffset} carries this
out explicitly, with a concrete spacing rule, for the seed
\[
 A_0=\{0,1,3,20,24,29\},
\]
whose fifteen positive differences are distinct.  (The value $20$ is one
convenient choice making the differences of the seed distinct; nothing
else about it is used.)

\paragraph{Organization.}
Section~\ref{sec:hyperfields} recalls hyperfields and quotient
hyperfields and proves that the cubic implication holds in the latter.
Section~\ref{sec:diffset} constructs the perfect difference set $D$,
Section~\ref{sec:plane} the cyclic plane, and
Section~\ref{sec:hyperfield} the hyperfield $\Hh$, including the
verification of all axioms.  Section~\ref{sec:counterexample} proves
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and deduces that $\Hh$ is not a quotient of a
field.  Credits for the ingredients are collected in
Section~\ref{sec:credits}.

\section{Hyperfields and quotient hyperfields}\label{sec:hyperfields}

\begin{definition}[Krasner {[Kr83]}]\label{def:hyperfield}
A \emph{commutative hyperfield} is a set $\Hh$ with two distinct
distinguished elements $0$ and $1$, a multiplication making
$\Hh\setminus\{0\}$ an abelian group with identity $1$ and satisfying
$0\cdot a=a\cdot 0=0$, and a hyperoperation $\bp$ (the
\emph{hyperaddition}) such that for all $a,b,c\in\Hh$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(H1)] $a\bp b=b\bp a$;
\item[(H2)] $(a\bp b)\bp c=a\bp(b\bp c)$, both sides being read with the
convention~\eqref{eq:union};
\item[(H3)] $0\bp a=\{a\}$;
\item[(H4)] there is a unique element $-a\in\Hh$ with $0\in a\bp(-a)$;
\item[(H5)] (reversibility) if $c\in a\bp b$, then $b\in c\bp(-a)$;
\item[(H6)] $a(b\bp c)=ab\bp ac$, where $a(b\bp c)=\{ad:d\in b\bp c\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

A set with a hyperoperation and an element $0$ satisfying (H1)--(H5) is
called a \emph{canonical hypergroup}, a term due to Mittas~[Mi72]; so a
hyperfield is a canonical hypergroup with a compatible multiplication.
A field is a hyperfield whose sums are singletons.  Hyperfields with noncommutative
multiplication are also considered in the literature; since the
question concerns an arbitrary hyperfield, a commutative counterexample
suffices, and ``hyperfield'' will mean commutative hyperfield below.

\begin{remark}[iterated sums]\label{rem:iterated}
The convention~\eqref{eq:union} makes $\bp$ a binary operation on the
nonempty subsets of $\Hh$, and (H1), (H2) make this operation
commutative and associative: for nonempty $A,B,C$,
\[
 (A\bp B)\bp C
 =\bigcup_{a\in A,\,b\in B,\,c\in C}(a\bp b)\bp c
 =\bigcup_{a\in A,\,b\in B,\,c\in C}a\bp(b\bp c)
 =A\bp(B\bp C).
\]
By the usual generalized associativity for an associative commutative
binary operation, an iterated sum $x_1\bp\cdots\bp x_n$ is independent
of the bracketing and of the order of the summands, and may be regrouped
freely.  In Section~\ref{sec:counterexample} we use this to write a
six-term sum as $(x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3)\bp(q\bp q\bp q)$.  Note also
$A\bp\{0\}=A$, by (H3).
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zero}
Let $\Hh$ be a hyperfield and $A,B\subseteq\Hh$ nonempty.  Then
$0\in A\bp B$ if and only if there is $a\in A$ with $-a\in B$.
In particular, if every element of $\Hh$ satisfies $-a=a$, then
$0\in A\bp B$ if and only if $A\cap B\neq\varnothing$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For elements, $0\in a\bp b$ holds if and only if $b=-a$, by the
uniqueness in (H4).  Now take the union over $a\in A$, $b\in B$.
\end{proof}

The second statement is the criterion of [CC11, Lemma~3.2], stated
there for vector spaces over the Krasner hyperfield $\mathbf K$, in
which likewise every element is its own negative.

\begin{example}[quotient hyperfields, Krasner {[Kr83]}]\label{ex:quotient}
Let $F$ be a field and $G\leq F^\times$ a subgroup of its multiplicative
group.  Let $F/G=\{0\}\cup\{uG:u\in F^\times\}$ be the set of orbits of
$G$ acting on $F$ by multiplication, and let $\pi\colon F\to F/G$ be the
orbit map, $\pi(0)=0$ and $\pi(u)=uG$ for $u\neq0$.  Multiplication on
$F/G$ is defined by $\pi(u)\pi(v)=\pi(uv)$, which is well defined, and
hyperaddition by
\[
 \pi(u)\bp\pi(v)
 =\bigl\{\pi(u'+v'):\ u'\in\pi^{-1}(\pi(u)),\ v'\in\pi^{-1}(\pi(v))\bigr\},
\]
the set of orbits of all sums of a representative of the first class
and a representative of the second.  Krasner~[Kr83] proved that $F/G$
is a commutative hyperfield.  Its negatives are $-\pi(u)=\pi(-u)$,
because $0=\pi(u+(-u))\in\pi(u)\bp\pi(-u)$ and negatives are unique by
(H4).  The fibres $\pi^{-1}(h)$ are $\{0\}$ and the cosets $uG$; they
are stable under multiplication by elements of $G$.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:quotient}
Let $F$ be a field, $G\leq F^\times$ a subgroup, and $x,y,z\in F/G$.
If $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, then
$0\in x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
We use two general facts about the orbit map $\pi$.

\smallskip\noindent
(i) \emph{If $u_1,\dots,u_n\in F$, then
$\pi(u_1+\cdots+u_n)\in\pi(u_1)\bp\cdots\bp\pi(u_n)$.}
For $n=1$ there is nothing to prove.  For $n\geq2$, the element
$u_1+\cdots+u_{n-1}$ is a representative of its own class and $u_n$ of
its own, so by the definition of $\bp$,
\[
 \pi(u_1+\cdots+u_n)\in\pi(u_1+\cdots+u_{n-1})\bp\pi(u_n),
\]
and $\pi(u_1+\cdots+u_{n-1})\in\pi(u_1)\bp\cdots\bp\pi(u_{n-1})$ by
induction; the convention~\eqref{eq:union} combines the two memberships.

\smallskip\noindent
(ii) \emph{If $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, then there are representatives
$u\in\pi^{-1}(x)$, $v\in\pi^{-1}(y)$, $w\in\pi^{-1}(z)$ with
$u+v+w=0$.}  By~\eqref{eq:union}, $0\in s\bp z$ for some $s\in x\bp y$.
By the definition of $\bp$, $0=\pi(s'+w)$ for some $s'\in\pi^{-1}(s)$
and $w\in\pi^{-1}(z)$; as $\pi^{-1}(0)=\{0\}$, this means $s'=-w$.
Also $s=\pi(u'+v')$ for some $u'\in\pi^{-1}(x)$, $v'\in\pi^{-1}(y)$.
If $u'+v'\neq0$, then $s'$ and $u'+v'$ lie in the same coset of $G$, so
$s'=(u'+v')g$ for some $g\in G$; put $u=u'g$ and $v=v'g$.  These still
represent $x$ and $y$, because fibres are $G$-stable, and
$u+v+w=s'+w=0$.  If $u'+v'=0$, then $s=0$, hence $s'=0$ and $w=0$, and
$u=u'$, $v=v'$ work.

\smallskip
Now let $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ and choose $u,v,w$ as in (ii).  The
identity~\eqref{eq:cubic} in the field $F$ gives
\[
 u^3+v^3+w^3+(-uvw)+(-uvw)+(-uvw)=0.
\]
Since $\pi$ is multiplicative and $\pi(-a)=-\pi(a)$
(Example~\ref{ex:quotient}), the six summands represent
$\pi(u^3)=x^3$, $\pi(v^3)=y^3$, $\pi(w^3)=z^3$ and
$\pi(-uvw)=-xyz$ (three times).  Applying (i) to them gives
\[
 0=\pi(0)\in x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

An \emph{isomorphism} of hyperfields is a bijection $f$ preserving $0$,
multiplication and hyperaddition (that is, $f(a\bp b)=f(a)\bp f(b)$ as
sets); it transports the cubic implication verbatim.  Together with
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient} will therefore
show that the hyperfield constructed below is not isomorphic to any
quotient $F/G$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:nonquotient}).

\section{A perfect difference set in the integers}\label{sec:diffset}

\begin{definition}\label{def:pds}
A subset $D\subseteq\Z$ is a \emph{perfect difference set} if the map
\[
 \{(d,e)\in D\times D:\ d\neq e\}\longrightarrow\Z\setminus\{0\},
 \qquad (d,e)\longmapsto d-e,
\]
is bijective; that is, every nonzero integer has exactly one expression
$d-e$ with $d,e\in D$.  For a finite set $A\subseteq\Z$ write
\[
 \Delta(A)=\{b-a:\ a,b\in A,\ a<b\}
\]
for its set of positive differences, and say that $A$ has
\emph{distinct differences} if the expressions $b-a$, for $a<b$ in $A$,
are pairwise distinct, i.e.\ if $|\Delta(A)|=\binom{|A|}{2}$.
\end{definition}

The terminology is Hall's~[Ha47]; the finite analogue, difference sets
modulo $n^2+n+1$, goes back to Singer~[Si38].  Recall from the
introduction that, by [Ha47, Theorem~3.1], every finite set with
distinct differences is contained in a perfect difference set of $\Z$.
We now carry this out for a specific seed and with an explicit spacing
rule; the result is Lemma~\ref{lem:diff}.
%% FLAG: the content of [Ha47, Theorem 3.1] was confirmed only through
%% secondary sources ([CC11, Example 4.7] and a later paper citing it as
%% the greedy extension of a finite Sidon set to an infinite perfect
%% difference set); the original 1947 text was not inspected, so it is
%% not claimed that Hall used the spacing rule N=2M+2m+1.

\paragraph{The seed.}
Let $A_0=\{0,1,3,20,24,29\}$.  Its positive differences, listed by
smaller element, are
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \text{from }0:& 1,\ 3,\ 20,\ 24,\ 29,\\
 \text{from }1:& 2,\ 19,\ 23,\ 28,\\
 \text{from }3:& 17,\ 21,\ 26,\\
 \text{from }20:& 4,\ 9,\\
 \text{from }24:& 5,
 \end{array}
\]
so that, in increasing order,
\[
 \Delta(A_0)=\{1,2,3,4,5,9,17,19,20,21,23,24,26,28,29\}.
\]
These are $15=\binom62$ distinct numbers, so $A_0$ has distinct
differences.  The roles of the seed elements were explained in the
introduction: $0,1,3$ make $x,y,z$ collinear, and $20,24,29$ make
$1,t^4,t^9$ collinear.

\paragraph{The extension step.}
Suppose a finite set $A_n\subseteq\Z_{\geq0}$ with distinct differences
has been constructed.  Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:parameters}
 M_n=\max A_n,\qquad
 m_n=\min\bigl(\Z_{>0}\setminus\Delta(A_n)\bigr),\qquad
 N_n=2M_n+2m_n+1,
\end{equation}
and set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:recursion}
 A_{n+1}=A_n\cup\{N_n,\ N_n+m_n\},\qquad
 D=\bigcup_{n\geq0}A_n.
\end{equation}
The integer $m_n$, the least positive difference not yet realized,
exists because $A_n$ is finite.  The idea of the step is simple: the two
new elements realize the missing difference $m_n$, and they are placed
so far to the right of $A_n$ that every other new difference exceeds
every old one.  For instance, $m_0=6$ and $N_0=2\cdot29+2\cdot6+1=71$,
so $A_1=A_0\cup\{71,77\}$; then $m_1=7$ and $N_1=169$, so
$A_2=A_1\cup\{169,176\}$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:diff}
Every $A_n$ has distinct differences.  The set $D$ is an infinite
perfect difference set with $D\subseteq\Z_{\geq0}$ and $\min D=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: $A_{n+1}$ has distinct differences.}
Abbreviate $A_n,M_n,m_n,N_n$ by $A,M,m,N$.  All elements of $A$ lie in
$[0,M]$, so every old difference is at most $M$.  The positive
differences of $A_{n+1}=A\cup\{N,N+m\}$ are the old ones, the
difference $(N+m)-N=m$ of the two new elements, and the mixed
differences
\[
 N-a\quad\text{and}\quad N+m-a\qquad(a\in A),
\]
which are positive because both new elements exceed $M$.  Since
$a\leq M$,
\[
 N-a\geq N-M=M+2m+1>\max\{M,m\},
\]
and the same bound holds for $N+m-a$.  Consequently no mixed difference
coincides with an old difference or with $m$, and $m$ is not an old
difference by its choice.  Within the family $\{N-a\}$, equal values
force equal $a$, and likewise within $\{N+m-a\}$.  A coincidence
$N-a=N+m-b$ between the two families would give $b-a=m$ with
$a,b\in A$, i.e.\ $m\in\Delta(A)$, contradicting the choice of $m$.
Thus all positive differences of $A_{n+1}$ are distinct, and by
induction every $A_n$ has distinct differences.

\emph{Step 2: every nonzero integer is a difference.}
By the minimality of $m_n$, the integers $1,\dots,m_n-1$ lie in
$\Delta(A_n)\subseteq\Delta(A_{n+1})$, and $m_n\in\Delta(A_{n+1})$ by
construction.  Hence $\{1,\dots,m_n\}\subseteq\Delta(A_{n+1})$ and
$m_{n+1}>m_n$.  The sequence $(m_n)$ is therefore unbounded, so every
positive integer $k$ satisfies $k<m_n$ for some $n$ and then
$k\in\Delta(A_n)$; thus $k=d-e$ with $d,e\in D$.  For negative $k$,
reverse the pair.

\emph{Step 3: uniqueness.}
Suppose $k=d-e=d'-e'$ with $(d,e)\neq(d',e')$ in $D\times D$ and, say,
$k>0$.  The sets $A_n$ increase with $n$, so $d,e,d',e'$ all lie in one
$A_n$, and $k$ would have two different expressions as a positive
difference in $A_n$, contrary to Step~1.  For $k<0$ negate both
expressions.

\emph{Step 4.}  Each step adjoins two elements larger than $M_n$, so $D$
is infinite; and $0\in A_0\subseteq D\subseteq\Z_{\geq0}$.
\end{proof}

\section{The cyclic plane}\label{sec:plane}

Let
\[
 P=\{t^j:\ j\in\Z\}
\]
be an infinite cyclic group with generator $t$, written
multiplicatively: $t^it^j=t^{i+j}$, with identity $1=t^0$, and distinct
exponents denote distinct elements.  Using the perfect difference set
$D$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:diff}, define for every $k\in\Z$ the \emph{line}
\[
 L_k=\{t^{k+d}:\ d\in D\}=t^k L_0 .
\]
Thus the lines are the translates of the single line $L_0=\{t^d:d\in D\}$.
Three points are \emph{collinear} if some line contains all of them, and
\emph{noncollinear} otherwise; a noncollinear triple $a,b,c$ is also
called a \emph{triangle} with \emph{vertices} $a,b,c$, and once (I1)
below is available its \emph{sides} are the lines
$L(a,b),L(a,c),L(b,c)$.  The following lemma collects everything that
will be used about the plane.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:incidence}
The points of $P$ and the lines $L_k$ have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(I1)] Any two distinct points of $P$ lie on exactly one line.
\item[(I2)] Any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.
\item[(I3)] The lines $L_k$, $k\in\Z$, are pairwise distinct.
\item[(I4)] Every line is infinite.  (Also, no line is all of $P$, since
$t^{k-1}\notin L_k$; this will not be needed.)
\item[(I5)] $t^rL_k=L_{k+r}$ for all $r,k\in\Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(I3) Since $\min D=0$, the least exponent occurring in $L_k$ is $k$.

(I1) Let $t^i\neq t^j$, so $i\neq j$.  The point $t^i$ lies on $L_k$ if
and only if $i-k\in D$.  Hence $L_k$ contains both points if and only if
$i-k=d$ and $j-k=e$ for some $d,e\in D$, and then $d-e=i-j\neq0$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:diff} there is exactly one pair $(d,e)\in D\times D$ with
$d-e=i-j$, so exactly one $k$, namely $k=i-d=j-e$, works; by (I3) this
means that exactly one line contains both points.

(I2) Let $k\neq\ell$.  A point $t^j$ lies on both $L_k$ and $L_\ell$ if
and only if $j-k=d\in D$ and $j-\ell=e\in D$, and then
$d-e=\ell-k\neq0$.  Again there is exactly one such pair $(d,e)$, hence
exactly one such $j=k+d$.

(I4) $D$ is infinite, and $-1\notin D$.

(I5) $t^r L_k=\{t^{r+k+d}:d\in D\}=L_{k+r}$.
\end{proof}

By (I1) we may write $L(a,b)$ for the unique line through two distinct
points $a,b$; thus, for $c\neq a,b$, the points $a,b,c$ are collinear if
and only if $c\in L(a,b)$.  A useful consequence of (I5): for distinct
$a,b\in P$ and $u\in P$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:translation}
 uL(a,b)=L(ua,ub),
\end{equation}
because $uL(a,b)$ is a line by (I5) and contains the distinct points
$ua,ub$.  Properties (I1) and (I2) say that $P$ with the lines $L_k$ is
a projective plane in the weak sense used in the introduction, and (I5)
says that the group $P$ acts on it by collineations.  Projective planes admitting a
cyclic group of collineations that acts sharply transitively on the
points (for any two points exactly one group element carries the first
to the second) are the \emph{cyclic planes} of Singer and Hall; in the
terminology of [CC11, \S3], a group structure on the point set for
which multiplications are collineations, such as our $P$, is a
two-sided incidence group of the plane.
%% FLAG: the phrase "two-sided incidence group" is recalled from
%% [CC11, Section 3] (Proposition 3.5 uses it); the exact wording of the
%% definition there was not re-checked against the source.

\section{The hyperfield}\label{sec:hyperfield}

Adjoin to $P$ a new element $0\notin P$ and put $\Hh=P\cup\{0\}$.
Extend the multiplication of $P$ by $0a=a0=0$ for all $a\in\Hh$; the
multiplicative identity is $1=t^0$, which is different from the new
element $0$.  Define the hyperaddition by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:addition}
 \begin{aligned}
 0\bp a&=a\bp0=\{a\} &&(a\in\Hh),\\
 a\bp a&=\{0,a\} &&(a\in P),\\
 a\bp b&=L(a,b)\setminus\{a,b\}
       &&(a,b\in P,\ a\neq b).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In words: the sum of two distinct points consists of the other points of
the line joining them, and the sum of a point with itself is the point
together with $0$.  This is Prenowitz's hyperaddition on a projective
geometry [Pr43], in the form used by Connes and Consani
[CC11, Proposition~3.1], who show that it yields a canonical hypergroup
whenever every line has at least four points, and that a two-sided
incidence group turns it into a hyperfield [CC11, Proposition~3.5].  We
do not rely on those results but verify the axioms directly; this also
makes visible exactly which incidence properties are used, namely
(I1), (I2), (I4) and~\eqref{eq:translation}.

Throughout this section we write, for $a,b,c\in\Hh$,
\[
 T(a,b,c)=(a\bp b)\bp c=\bigcup_{d\in a\bp b}(d\bp c)
\]
for the left-bracketed triple sum.  The first lemma is the heart of the
associativity proof: for a triangle the triple sum has a description
that is visibly symmetric in the three summands.  The formula also
appears in the proof of [CC11, Proposition~3.1].

\begin{lemma}[triangle formula]\label{lem:triangle}
For three noncollinear points $a,b,c\in P$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangle}
 T(a,b,c)=(a\bp b)\bp c
 =P\setminus\bigl(L(a,b)\cup L(a,c)\cup L(b,c)\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular $0\notin T(a,b,c)$, and $T(a,b,c)$ is disjoint from the
three sides of the triangle $abc$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Noncollinear points are distinct, and $c\notin L(a,b)$,
$b\notin L(a,c)$, $a\notin L(b,c)$; so the three sides are three distinct
lines, and by (I2) any two of them meet only in their common vertex.

\emph{The left side is contained in the right side.}
Let $r\in T(a,b,c)$.  Then $r\in d\bp c$ for some
$d\in a\bp b=L(a,b)\setminus\{a,b\}$.  Since $c\notin L(a,b)$ we have
$d\neq c$, so $d\bp c=L(d,c)\setminus\{d,c\}$; in particular $r\neq0$,
$r\in P$, and $r\neq d,c$.  The line $L(d,c)$ is different from
$L(a,b)$ (it contains $c$), so it meets $L(a,b)$ only in $d$, by (I2);
as $r\neq d$, $r\notin L(a,b)$.  Next, $d\notin L(a,c)$: the lines
$L(a,c)$ and $L(a,b)$ are distinct and meet only in $a$, while
$d\in L(a,b)$ and $d\neq a$.  Hence $L(d,c)\neq L(a,c)$, these two
lines meet only in $c$, and $r\neq c$ gives $r\notin L(a,c)$.  The same
argument with $b$ in place of $a$ gives $r\notin L(b,c)$.

\emph{The right side is contained in the left side.}
Let $r\in P$ lie on none of the three sides.  Then $r\neq c$, and the
line $L(c,r)$ is different from $L(a,b)$ because $c\notin L(a,b)$; by
(I2) the two lines meet in exactly one point $d$.  If $d$ were equal to
$a$, then $a\in L(c,r)$ would force $L(c,r)=L(a,c)$ by (I1), placing
$r$ on the side $L(a,c)$; so $d\neq a$, and likewise $d\neq b$.  Also
$d\neq c$ (as $c\notin L(a,b)$) and $d\neq r$ (as $r\notin L(a,b)$).
Therefore $d\in L(a,b)\setminus\{a,b\}=a\bp b$, and
$r\in L(c,r)\setminus\{d,c\}=L(d,c)\setminus\{d,c\}=d\bp c$, so
$r\in T(a,b,c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:hyperfield}
With the multiplication and hyperaddition above, $\Hh$ is a commutative
hyperfield in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:hyperfield}.  Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zero}
 0\in a\bp b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a=b\qquad(a,b\in\Hh),
\end{equation}
so every element is its own negative, $-a=a$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All sums are nonempty: a line minus two points is nonempty by (I4).
Commutativity (H1) and the neutrality of $0$ (H3) are built into
\eqref{eq:addition}.

\emph{Negatives (H4).}  Inspecting the three rules of
\eqref{eq:addition} gives~\eqref{eq:zero}: $0$ lies in $a\bp a$ for
every $a$ (including $a=0$), in $0\bp b=\{b\}$ only if $b=0$, and in
$L(a,b)\setminus\{a,b\}\subseteq P$ never.  Thus $a$ itself is the
unique element $-a$ with $0\in a\bp(-a)$.

\emph{Reversibility (H5).}  Since $-a=a$, we must show that
$c\in a\bp b$ implies $b\in c\bp a$; we show in fact that the two
conditions
\[
 c\in a\bp b\qquad\text{and}\qquad b\in c\bp a
\]
are equivalent.  If one of $a,b,c$ is $0$, both conditions say that the
other two are equal: for $a=0$ by (H3), for $b=0$ by (H3)
and~\eqref{eq:zero}, and for $c=0$ by~\eqref{eq:zero} and (H3).  Let
$a,b,c\in P$.  If $a=b=c$, both conditions hold ($a\in a\bp a$).  If
exactly two of them are equal, both conditions fail: a sum
$u\bp u=\{0,u\}$ never contains a point different from $u$, and a sum
$u\bp v$ with $u\neq v$ contains neither $u$ nor $v$.  If $a,b,c$ are
distinct, both conditions say that $a,b,c$ are collinear, by (I1).

\emph{Associativity (H2).}  The commutativity part of
Remark~\ref{rem:iterated} uses only (H1), so
\[
 a\bp(b\bp c)=(b\bp c)\bp a=T(b,c,a).
\]
Hence (H2) follows once we show that $T(a,b,c)$ depends only on the
multiset $\{a,b,c\}$ and not on the order of the summands.  A triple
either contains $0$, or lies in $P^3$ and has three equal summands,
exactly two equal summands, or three distinct summands, the last being
collinear or not; we compute $T$ in each of these five cases.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{A zero summand.}  By (H3) and $A\bp\{0\}=A$,
$T(0,a,b)=T(a,0,b)=T(a,b,0)=a\bp b$, which is symmetric in $a,b$.
\item \emph{Three equal nonzero summands $a,a,a$.}
$T(a,a,a)=\{0,a\}\bp a=(0\bp a)\cup(a\bp a)=\{0,a\}$.
\item \emph{Exactly two equal summands.}  Let the summands be $a,a,b$
with $a\neq b$ in $P$, in any order, and put $L=L(a,b)$.  Then
\[
 T(a,a,b)=\{0,a\}\bp b=\{b\}\cup\bigl(L\setminus\{a,b\}\bigr)
 =L\setminus\{a\},
\]
and, since $d\bp a=L\setminus\{d,a\}$ for $d\in L\setminus\{a,b\}$,
\[
 T(a,b,a)=T(b,a,a)
 =\bigcup_{d\in L\setminus\{a,b\}}\bigl(L\setminus\{a,d\}\bigr)
 =L\setminus\{a\}.
\]
For the last equality: the union is contained in $L\setminus\{a\}$, and
a point $r\in L\setminus\{a\}$ is retained by choosing
$d\in L\setminus\{a,b,r\}$, which is possible because $L$ is infinite
(I4).  So all three orderings give $L(a,b)\setminus\{a\}$.
\item \emph{Three distinct collinear summands} $a,b,c$ on a line $L$.
Here $a\bp b=L\setminus\{a,b\}$, and for $d\in L\setminus\{a,b\}$ the
summand $d\bp c$ is $\{0,c\}$ if $d=c$ and $L\setminus\{d,c\}$ if
$d\neq c$ (because then $L(d,c)=L$).  Hence
\[
 T(a,b,c)=\{0,c\}\cup\bigcup_{d\in L\setminus\{a,b,c\}}
 \bigl(L\setminus\{d,c\}\bigr)=\{0,c\}\cup\bigl(L\setminus\{c\}\bigr)
 =L\cup\{0\},
\]
where a point $r\in L\setminus\{c\}$ is retained by choosing
$d\in L\setminus\{a,b,c,r\}$, again possible by (I4).  The result
$L\cup\{0\}$ depends only on the line $L$, hence only on the multiset
$\{a,b,c\}$.
\item \emph{Three noncollinear summands.}  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}, $T(a,b,c)$ is the complement in $P$ of the
union of the three sides, which is symmetric in $a,b,c$.
\end{itemize}
This proves (H2).  Thus $(\Hh,\bp,0)$ is a canonical hypergroup.  (It
also satisfies $a\bp\Hh=\Hh$, a condition some authors include: given
$b$, pick $c\in b\bp a$; then $b\in c\bp a$ by (H5).)

\emph{Multiplication and distributivity (H6).}  The nonzero elements
form the abelian group $P$ with identity $1\neq0$, and $0$ is
absorbing.  Let $u\in P$.  For distinct $a,b\in P$,
\eqref{eq:translation} gives
\[
 u(a\bp b)=uL(a,b)\setminus\{ua,ub\}=L(ua,ub)\setminus\{ua,ub\}
 =ua\bp ub,
\]
using that multiplication by $u$ is a bijection of $P$.  For equal
nonzero summands, $u\{0,a\}=\{0,ua\}=ua\bp ua$; if a summand is $0$,
both sides of (H6) are the singleton of the product of $u$ with the
other summand.  Finally, for $u=0$ both sides of (H6) equal $\{0\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[where the size of the lines enters]\label{rem:linesize}
Infiniteness of the lines was used only to choose a point of a line
outside a prescribed set of at most four points; so the proof works
verbatim for any plane satisfying (I1), (I2), whose point set is an
abelian group acting by collineations as in (I5), and in which every
line has at least five points.  Connes and Consani show that four points per
line suffice for the hypergroup axioms [CC11, Proposition~3.1]; on a
four-point line $L=\{a,b,c,d\}$ one computes
$a\bp b\bp c=\{0,a,b,c\}$ rather than $L\cup\{0\}$, still a symmetric
expression.
With only three points per line the rule~\eqref{eq:addition} is not
associative: on the line $\{a,b,c\}$ one finds
$(a\bp b)\bp c=c\bp c=\{0,c\}$ but $a\bp(b\bp c)=a\bp a=\{0,a\}$.
\end{remark}

\section{The counterexample}\label{sec:counterexample}

We now prove Theorem~\ref{thm:main} for the hyperfield $\Hh$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:hyperfield} and the elements
\[
 x=1,\qquad y=t,\qquad z=t^3 .
\]
Recall that $D\supseteq A_0=\{0,1,3,20,24,29\}$ and that $-a=a$ for
every $a\in\Hh$, so the summands of the conclusion are
\[
 x^3=1,\qquad y^3=t^3,\qquad z^3=t^9,\qquad -xyz=xyz=t^4=:q .
\]

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:counterexample}
In $\Hh$, with $x=1$, $y=t$, $z=t^3$,
\[
 0\in x\bp y\bp z
 \qquad\text{but}\qquad
 0\notin x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: the hypothesis holds.}  Since $0,1,3\in D$, the three
distinct points $1,t,t^3$ lie on $L_0$.  In particular
$t^3\in L(1,t)\setminus\{1,t\}=1\bp t$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hypothesis}
 0\in t^3\bp t^3\subseteq(1\bp t)\bp t^3=x\bp y\bp z .
\end{equation}
(In fact $x\bp y\bp z=L_0\cup\{0\}$ by the collinear case in the proof
of Proposition~\ref{prop:hyperfield}, but~\eqref{eq:hypothesis} is all
we need.)

\emph{Step 2: the cubes are noncollinear, and $q$ lies on a side of
their triangle.}  Since $20,24,29\in D$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:specialline}
 1=t^{-20+20},\quad q=t^4=t^{-20+24},\quad t^9=t^{-20+29}\ \in\ L_{-20},
\end{equation}
so $L_{-20}=L(1,t^9)$ by (I1).  On the other hand $23\notin D$:
otherwise the two distinct pairs $(23,20)$ and $(3,0)$ in $D\times D$
would both represent $3=23-20=3-0$, contradicting the uniqueness in
Lemma~\ref{lem:diff}.  Hence $t^3=t^{-20+23}\notin L_{-20}=L(1,t^9)$,
which by (I1) says precisely that $1,t^3,t^9$ are noncollinear.

\emph{Step 3: the conclusion fails.}  Put
\[
 S=x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3=(1\bp t^3)\bp t^9=T(1,t^3,t^9).
\]
By Step~2 and the triangle formula (Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}), $S$
contains neither $0$ nor any point of the side $L(1,t^9)=L_{-20}$.
By~\eqref{eq:specialline}, $q\in L_{-20}$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:disjoint}
 S\cap\{0,q\}=\varnothing .
\end{equation}
Next, by~\eqref{eq:addition},
\[
 q\bp q\bp q=\{0,q\}\bp q=(0\bp q)\cup(q\bp q)=\{q\}\cup\{0,q\}=\{0,q\}.
\]
By Remark~\ref{rem:iterated} the six-term sum may be regrouped:
\[
 x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp q\bp q\bp q
 =(x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3)\bp(q\bp q\bp q)=S\bp\{0,q\}.
\]
Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:zero} together with $-a=a$ gives, for subsets
$A,B\subseteq\Hh$, that $0\in A\bp B$ if and only if
$A\cap B\neq\varnothing$.  Applied to $A=S$ and $B=\{0,q\}$,
\eqref{eq:disjoint} yields
\[
 0\notin S\bp\{0,q\}
 =x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz).
\]
Together with~\eqref{eq:hypothesis} this proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample} establishes Theorem~\ref{thm:main}:
$\Hh$ is countably infinite, since $P\cong\Z$, and commutative by
Proposition~\ref{prop:hyperfield}.  So the answer to the question is
\textbf{no}.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:nonquotient}
The hyperfield $\Hh$ is not isomorphic to a quotient hyperfield $F/G$
of a field $F$ by a subgroup $G\leq F^\times$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient} every quotient hyperfield satisfies
the cubic implication, an isomorphism of hyperfields transports the
implication, and $\Hh$ violates it by Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:context}
Hyperfields that are not quotients of fields were first constructed by
Massouros~[Ma85], by a different method.  Hyperfields attached to
infinite cyclic planes built from Hall's difference sets appear in
[CC11, Example~4.7].  For quotient hyperfields $F/G$ satisfying
$a\bp a=\{0,a\}$ for all $a$ (a property our $\Hh$ shares,
by~\eqref{eq:addition}), the projective geometry attached to the
hyperaddition, whose lines are the sets $\{a,b\}\cup(a\bp b)$ for
distinct nonzero $a,b$ (for our $\Hh$ these are exactly the lines
$L(a,b)$), is Desarguesian; [KB25, Example~2.6(4) and Remark~4.3(3)]
contrasts such quotients with a hyperfield built on an infinite cyclic
group whose plane is non-Desarguesian, and thereby separates general
hyperfields from quotients of fields.
Corollary~\ref{cor:nonquotient} gives, for the specific $\Hh$
constructed here, a direct elementary verification that involves no
Desargues configuration: the cubic implication is a first-order
statement true in every $F/G$ and false in $\Hh$.
%% FLAG: the scope of the Desarguesian assertion (quotient hyperfields
%% with a+a={0,a} only, not arbitrary quotients) follows the critic's
%% reading of the published text of [KB25, Example 2.6(4), Remark
%% 4.3(3)]; the editor did not inspect that text directly.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[what the example shows]
For distinct $x,y,z\in P$ the hypothesis $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ is the
collinearity of $x,y,z$ (by the collinear and noncollinear cases in the
proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:hyperfield}), and, since cubing is
injective on $P\cong\Z$ so that the cubes are distinct, the conclusion
holds if the cubes are collinear and otherwise holds exactly when $xyz$
avoids all three sides of the cube triangle, by the argument of
Step~3.  In a field,
or in a quotient of a field, the two conditions are linked by the
identity~\eqref{eq:cubic}.  In the cyclic plane of a perfect difference
set the two conditions are independent, and the construction exploits
this: the seed elements $0,1,3\in D$ make $x,y,z$ collinear, so the
hypothesis holds; the seed elements $20,24,29\in D$ place $xyz=t^4$ on
the side $L(1,t^9)$ of the cube triangle, so the conclusion fails; and
the uniqueness of differences built into $D$ excludes $23\in D$ (which
would duplicate the difference $3=23-20=3-0$) and so keeps the cubes
noncollinear.
\end{remark}

\section{Background and credits}\label{sec:credits}

None of the ingredients is new: the hyperfield axioms and the quotient
hyperfields $F/G$ are Krasner's [Kr83], the term canonical hypergroup
is Mittas's [Mi72], the hyperaddition ``third points of the joining
line'' is Prenowitz's [Pr43] and was combined with an incidence group
to produce hyperfields by Connes and Consani [CC11, \S3, Example~4.7],
and perfect difference sets and cyclic planes are due to Singer~[Si38]
(finite case) and Hall~[Ha47] (the group $\Z$), of whose Theorem~3.1
Lemma~\ref{lem:diff} is an explicit instance.
Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient} is an elementary observation about
quotient hyperfields.  What appears to be new is the counterexample
itself: the choice of the seed $A_0$, the resulting incidence
configuration, and the failure of the cubic implication; a literature
search did not locate the question or an earlier answer.

\begin{abstract}
An \(L\)-space knot is a knot in \(S^3\) with a non-trivial Dehn surgery
whose Heegaard Floer homology is as small as its first homology allows.
We show that every Dehn surgery on an \(L\)-space knot has at most two
non-trivial prime summands. The proof combines published results on
reducible surgeries (\(L\)-space knots are fibered, by Ni; a reducible
surgery on a hyperbolic knot with a positive \(L\)-space surgery has slope
\(2g-1\), by Hom--Lidman--Zufelt; the Cabling Conjecture holds for
non-trivial non-hyperbolic knots, by Moser and Scharlemann; Gordon's
formula for
surgery on a cable; the Gordon--Luecke theorem on non-integral surgeries)
with an elementary group-theoretic obstruction: if a \(p/q\)-surgery on a
fibered knot of genus \(g\) has a non-trivial integer homology sphere
summand, then \(|p|\le g\). The obstruction is proved by estimating the
minimal number of generators of the commutator subgroup of the
fundamental group in two ways, through the universal abelian cover and
Grushko's theorem on free products on one side and through the
fundamental group of the fiber surface on the other.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Dehn surgery along a knot \(K\subset S^3\) produces a closed oriented
\(3\)-manifold \(\Surg{r}{K}\) for every slope
\(r\in\Q\cup\{\infty\}\) (notation is recalled in
Section~\ref{sec:surgery}). By the Kneser--Milnor theorem, every closed
oriented \(3\)-manifold is a connected sum of prime manifolds, unique up to
order, and a basic question in Dehn surgery theory is how complicated this
decomposition can be for a surgery on a knot. For a non-trivial knot
\(K\subset S^3\), the Cabling Conjecture of Gonz\'alez-Acu\~na and Short
\cite{GAS1986} predicts that \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is reducible only when
\(K\) is a cable knot and \(r\) is the slope of the cabling annulus (the
unknot must be excluded, since its \(0\)-surgery is \(S^1\times S^2\)); in
that case the surgery is a lens space connected-summed
with a surgery on the companion knot (Gordon \cite{Gordon1983}), and the
latter surgery is prime, because its slope is non-integral (Gordon--Luecke
\cite{GordonLuecke1987}) or because the companion is the unknot, so the
conjecture predicts in particular that a
surgery on a knot in \(S^3\) never has three non-trivial prime summands.
The conjecture is known for
torus knots (Moser \cite{Moser1971}) and for satellite knots (Scharlemann
\cite{Scharlemann1990}), and it is open for hyperbolic knots. Without any
hypothesis on the knot, Howie \cite{Howie2002} showed that at most two
prime summands of a surgery on a knot in \(S^3\) can have non-zero first
homology, so a third summand would have to be an integer homology sphere;
see also \cite{Howie2010}.

This note answers the question for knots satisfying a strong
Heegaard Floer restriction. An \emph{\(L\)-space} is a rational homology
sphere \(Y\) whose Heegaard Floer homology \(\HFhat(Y)\) has the smallest
possible dimension, namely \(|H_1(Y;\Z)|\); lens spaces are examples. A knot
\(K\subset S^3\) is an \emph{\(L\)-space knot} if \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is an
\(L\)-space for some slope \(r\neq\infty\). We allow \(r\) of either sign;
some authors require \(r>0\), and we explain at the end of
Section~\ref{sec:Lspace} and in Step~1 of Section~\ref{sec:proof} why the
two conventions lead to the same theorem. These notions are recalled in
Section~\ref{sec:Lspace}. Torus knots are \(L\)-space knots, since
suitable surgeries on them are lens spaces \cite{Moser1971}.

We count the prime summands of a manifold other than \(S^3\) in its
Kneser--Milnor decomposition, and we say that \(S^3\) has none
(Section~\ref{sec:prime}); these are its \emph{non-trivial prime
summands}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be an \(L\)-space knot. For every slope
\(r\in\Q\cup\{\infty\}\), the manifold \(\Surg{r}{K}\) has at most two
non-trivial prime summands.
\end{theorem}

The \(L\)-space hypothesis enters the proof at exactly two points, each
through a published theorem: \(L\)-space knots are fibered (Ni
\cite{Ni2007}), and a reducible surgery on a \emph{hyperbolic} knot
admitting a positive \(L\)-space surgery has slope exactly \(2g-1\), where
\(g\) is the genus of the knot (Hom--Lidman--Zufelt \cite[Theorem~1.3]{HLZ2015}).
For non-trivial non-hyperbolic knots no Floer-theoretic input is needed,
because the Cabling Conjecture is a theorem there. The argument does not identify
the reducible surgery itself, and it does not prove the Cabling
Conjecture for hyperbolic \(L\)-space knots; see Remark~\ref{rem:notproved}.
The main ingredient we prove here is the following statement about
fibered knots, established in Section~\ref{sec:rank} as
Proposition~\ref{prop:large}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:fibered}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be a fibered knot of genus \(g\geq1\), and let
\(p/q\) be a slope with \(p\neq0\) and \(|p|\geq 2g-1\). Then
\(\Surg{p/q}{K}\) has at most two non-trivial prime summands.
\end{theorem}

\paragraph{Strategy.}
Suppose that \(M=\Surg{p/q}{K}\) has three non-trivial prime summands.
By Howie's theorem one of them, call it \(\Sigma\), has
\(H_1(\Sigma;\Z)=0\), so \(M\cong X\#\Sigma\) with \(\Sigma\) an integer
homology sphere other than \(S^3\) and \(H_1(X;\Z)\cong H_1(M;\Z)\cong\Z/|p|\).
Let \(G=\pi_1(M)\) and let \(G'\) be its commutator subgroup. We compute
the minimal number of generators \(\rk(G')\) in two ways.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{From above}, via the fiber. The group \(G\) is a quotient of
the knot group \(\pi_1(E_K)\), where \(E_K\) is the knot exterior, whose
commutator subgroup is the
fundamental group of the fiber surface, a free group of rank \(2g\). An
epimorphism maps commutator subgroups onto commutator subgroups, so
\(\rk(G')\leq 2g\) (Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber}).
\item \emph{From below}, via the universal abelian cover. The subgroup
\(G'\) is the fundamental group of the \(|p|\)-fold cover
\(\widetilde M\to M\) with deck group \(G/G'=H_1(M;\Z)\). Because
\(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is perfect, it maps trivially to the deck group, so the
punctured copy of \(\Sigma\) inside \(M\) lifts to \(|p|\) disjoint copies,
and \(\widetilde M\cong\widetilde X\#\Sigma^{\#|p|}\). Since
\(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is non-trivial and perfect it is not cyclic, so it needs
at least two generators, and Grushko's theorem gives
\(\rk(G')\geq 2|p|\) (Lemma~\ref{lem:cover}).
\end{itemize}
Hence \(|p|\leq g\). This is incompatible with \(|p|\geq 2g-1\) unless
\(g=1\) and \(|p|=1\), an endpoint case that is excluded by a direct
application of Grushko's theorem to the perfect group \(G\).

Theorem~\ref{thm:main} then follows by Thurston's trichotomy, according
to which every non-trivial knot is a torus knot, a satellite knot or
hyperbolic (Section~\ref{sec:types}). For a hyperbolic \(L\)-space knot, Ni's theorem and the Hom--Lidman--Zufelt
theorem put every reducible surgery exactly in the range of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fibered}; for a torus or satellite knot the Cabling
Conjecture, Gordon's formula for surgery on a cable, and the
Gordon--Luecke theorem that non-integral surgeries are irreducible leave
room for at most two summands.

\paragraph{Outline.}
Section~\ref{sec:background} fixes
conventions and recalls the standard facts we use,
Section~\ref{sec:rank} proves the group-rank obstruction,
Section~\ref{sec:inputs} states the published theorems that are used as
black boxes, Section~\ref{sec:proof} proves Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, and
Section~\ref{sec:comments} discusses what the argument does and does not
show.

A genus bound of the shape \(|p|\leq g\) for surgeries with a non-trivial
integer homology sphere summand is attributed to Gonz\'alez-Acu\~na and
Short \cite[Proposition~1.4]{GAS1986} in \cite[Theorem~1.2]{BodishDeYeso},
in the case where the complementary summand \(X\) is a lens space. The
case needed here has \(X\) non-prime, so we prove Lemma~\ref{lem:cover}
for an arbitrary complementary summand. Related statements about
homology sphere summands of surgeries on \(L\)-space knots appear in
\cite[Section~4]{BodishDeYeso}. We make no claim of priority for
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}; the aim of this note is a complete and
self-contained argument modulo the cited theorems.

\section{Conventions and background}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{Dehn surgery}\label{sec:surgery}

Throughout, \(K\subset S^3\) is a tame knot, \(\nbd K\) is a closed
tubular neighbourhood of \(K\), and \(E_K=S^3\setminus\Int\nbd K\) is the
\emph{exterior} of \(K\), a compact oriented \(3\)-manifold with torus
boundary. On \(\partial E_K=\partial\nbd K\) we fix the \emph{meridian}
\(\mu\), a simple closed curve bounding a disc in \(\nbd K\), and the
\emph{preferred longitude} \(\lambda\), a simple closed curve isotopic to
\(K\) in \(\nbd K\) and null-homologous in \(E_K\) (it is the boundary of
a Seifert surface for \(K\)). A \emph{slope} is an isotopy class of
unoriented essential simple closed curves on \(\partial E_K\). The curve
homologous to \(p\mu+q\lambda\), with \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), determines the
slope \(p/q\in\Q\cup\{\infty\}\), where \(\infty=1/0\) is the meridional
slope; for finite slopes we normalise \(q>0\), so that
\(p\in\Z\) is determined.

The \emph{Dehn surgery} on \(K\) with slope \(r\) is the closed oriented
\(3\)-manifold
\[
 \Surg{r}{K}=E_K\cup_\varphi (S^1\times D^2),
\]
where the gluing homeomorphism
\(\varphi\colon\partial(S^1\times D^2)\to\partial E_K\) sends the meridian
\(\{*\}\times\partial D^2\) of the solid torus to a curve of slope \(r\),
and the orientation extends that of \(E_K\subset S^3\). Its
homeomorphism type depends only on \(r\). We use the following standard
facts.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(S1)] \(\Surg{\infty}{K}=S^3\), since filling along the meridian
undoes the removal of \(\nbd K\).
\item[(S2)] \(H_1(E_K;\Z)\cong\Z\), generated by \(\mu\), and \(\lambda=0\)
in \(H_1(E_K;\Z)\). Filling along \(p\mu+q\lambda\) kills the class
\(p[\mu]\), so
\[
 H_1(\Surg{p/q}{K};\Z)\cong\Z/|p|\Z,
\]
which is to be read as \(\Z\) when \(p=0\). In particular
\(\Surg{p/q}{K}\) is a rational homology sphere if and only if \(p\neq0\).
\item[(S3)] By van Kampen's theorem,
\(\pi_1(\Surg{p/q}{K})\cong\pi_1(E_K)/\langle\!\langle\gamma_{p/q}\rangle\!\rangle\),
the quotient by the normal closure of the element \(\gamma_{p/q}\) of
\(\pi_1(E_K)\) represented by the filling curve of slope \(p/q\) (the
elements of \(\pi_1(E_K)\) represented by \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\) are
again denoted \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\)). Applied to \(p/q=\infty\) this
gives
\(\pi_1(E_K)/\langle\!\langle\mu\rangle\!\rangle\cong\pi_1(S^3)=1\): the
knot group is normally generated by a meridian.
\item[(S4)] Let \(\overline K\) be the mirror image of \(K\). A reflection
of \(S^3\) carrying \(K\) to \(\overline K\) preserves meridians and
preferred longitudes but reverses the intersection pairing on the
boundary torus, so it carries the slope \(r\) of \(K\) to the slope
\(-r\) of \(\overline K\) and induces an orientation-reversing
homeomorphism \(\Surg{r}{K}\to\Surg{-r}{\overline K}\); equivalently,
there is an orientation-preserving identification
\(\Surg{-r}{\overline K}\cong-\Surg{r}{K}\), where \(-M\) denotes \(M\)
with the opposite orientation.
\item[(S5)] For the unknot \(U\), \(\Surg{p/q}{U}\) is a lens space
with first homology of order \(|p|\) (namely \(L(p,q)\) up to
orientation) when \(|p|\geq2\), is \(S^3\) when \(|p|=1\), and is
\(S^1\times S^2\) when \(p=0\). Here, for \(p\geq2\) (negative \(p\)
differs only by orientation), \(L(p,q)\) denotes the quotient of the
unit sphere \(S^3\subset\mathbb C^2\) by the free action of \(\Z/p\Z\)
generated by \((z,w)\mapsto(\zeta z,\zeta^{q}w)\), \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/p}\);
it has \(H_1(L(p,q);\Z)\cong\Z/p\Z\) and universal cover \(S^3\).
Orientation conventions for lens spaces play no role in this note, since
only the number of prime summands is counted.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Prime decomposition}\label{sec:prime}

Let \(M\) be a closed connected oriented \(3\)-manifold. \(M\) is
\emph{irreducible} if every embedded \(2\)-sphere in \(M\) bounds a
\(3\)-ball, and \emph{reducible} otherwise. \(M\) is \emph{prime} if
\(M\cong M_1\#M_2\) implies \(M_1\cong S^3\) or \(M_2\cong S^3\). An
irreducible manifold is prime, and conversely a prime closed orientable
\(3\)-manifold is either irreducible or homeomorphic to \(S^1\times S^2\)
\cite[\S1.1]{Hatcher3M}. Thus for a rational homology sphere, prime and
irreducible are the same thing, and non-prime is the same as reducible.

If a covering space of \(M\) is irreducible, so is \(M\)
\cite[Proposition~1.6]{Hatcher3M}; by Alexander's theorem
\cite[\S1.1]{Hatcher3M}, \(S^3\) and \(\R^3\) are irreducible. Hence
lens spaces, which are covered by \(S^3\), are irreducible, and so is
any closed \(3\)-manifold with universal cover \(\R^3\).

The Kneser--Milnor theorem \cite[Theorem~1.5]{Hatcher3M} states that
every closed oriented \(3\)-manifold \(M\not\cong S^3\) is a connected sum
\(M\cong M_1\#\cdots\#M_k\) of prime manifolds \(M_i\not\cong S^3\), and
that the collection \(\{M_i\}\) is unique up to order and
orientation-preserving homeomorphism. We call \(M_1,\dots,M_k\) the
\emph{non-trivial prime summands} of \(M\); by uniqueness their number
\(k\) is an invariant of \(M\), and we set \(k=0\) for \(M\cong S^3\).
Reversing the orientation of \(M\) reverses that of each \(M_i\), so
\(M\) and \(-M\) have the same number of non-trivial prime summands.
By van Kampen's theorem, for any connected sum of closed oriented
\(3\)-manifolds \(N_1,\dots,N_k\) (prime or not),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vk}
 \pi_1(N_1\#\cdots\#N_k)\cong\pi_1(N_1)*\cdots*\pi_1(N_k),
 \qquad
 H_1(N_1\#\cdots\#N_k;\Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^k H_1(N_i;\Z),
\end{equation}
since the connected sum is formed by gluing punctured copies of the
\(N_i\) along \(2\)-spheres, and removing a ball from a \(3\)-manifold
does not change its fundamental group.

A closed connected oriented \(3\)-manifold \(\Sigma\) with
\(H_1(\Sigma;\Z)=0\) is called an \emph{integer homology sphere}; by
Poincar\'e duality and the universal coefficient theorem,
\(H_*(\Sigma;\Z)\cong H_*(S^3;\Z)\).

\subsection{Torus, satellite and hyperbolic knots; cables}\label{sec:types}

A non-trivial knot \(K\subset S^3\) is a \emph{torus knot} if it can be
isotoped onto the boundary of a standardly embedded solid torus; it is a
\emph{satellite knot} if \(E_K\) contains an incompressible torus (an
embedded torus whose fundamental group injects into \(\pi_1(E_K)\)) that
is not parallel to \(\partial E_K\); and it is \emph{hyperbolic} if
\(S^3\setminus K\) admits a complete hyperbolic metric of finite volume.
By Thurston's hyperbolization theorem, every non-trivial knot is of
exactly one of these three types \cite[Corollary~2.5]{Thurston1982}.
Composite knots are satellite knots: if \(K=K_1\#K_2\) with both
summands non-trivial, the boundary of a regular neighbourhood of the
union of \(K\) with a ball containing the \(K_2\) summand is a torus in
\(E_K\), knotted like \(K_1\), which is incompressible and not
boundary-parallel (the ``swallow--follow'' torus).

Let \(J\subset S^3\) be a knot, with meridian \(\mu_J\) and preferred
longitude \(\lambda_J\) on \(\partial\nbd J\), and let \(w\geq2\) and
\(t\) be coprime integers (so \(t\neq0\)). The \emph{\((w,t)\)-cable} of
\(J\) is the knot
\[
 C_{w,t}(J)\subset\partial\nbd J\subset S^3
\]
given by a simple closed curve on \(\partial\nbd J\) homologous to
\(t\mu_J+w\lambda_J\) there. Its image in \(H_1(\nbd J;\Z)\cong\Z\) is
\(w\) times the generator, so \(w\) is the \emph{winding number} of the
cable. If \(J\) is the unknot, \(C_{w,t}(J)\) is the torus knot
\(T_{w,t}\); if \(J\) is non-trivial, \(C_{w,t}(J)\) is a satellite knot
with companion \(J\). We call \(wt\) the \emph{cabling slope} of
\(C_{w,t}(J)\): it is the framing of the cable induced by the torus
\(\partial\nbd J\), and the annulus
\(\partial\nbd J\setminus\Int\nbd C_{w,t}(J)\) has both boundary curves of
slope \(wt\) on \(\partial\nbd C_{w,t}(J)\). (Several indexing
conventions for cables are in use; we fix the one above, in which the
first index is the winding number.)

\subsection{Fibered knots}\label{sec:fibered}

A knot \(K\) is \emph{fibered} if \(E_K\) is the total space of a fiber
bundle over \(S^1\) whose fibers are Seifert surfaces for \(K\), that is,
compact connected oriented surfaces \(F\subset E_K\) with
\(\partial F=\lambda\). The fiber then realises the minimal genus of a
Seifert surface for \(K\), so its genus is the \emph{genus} \(g=g(K)\)
of the knot, and \(g\geq1\) when \(K\) is non-trivial. Since \(F\) is a
compact connected orientable surface of genus \(g\) with one boundary
component, it deformation retracts onto a wedge of \(2g\) circles, and
\(\pi_1(F)\) is a free group \(F_{2g}\) of rank \(2g\). The long exact
homotopy sequence of the bundle gives a short exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fibration}
 1\longrightarrow\pi_1(F)\longrightarrow\pi_1(E_K)
 \longrightarrow\pi_1(S^1)=\Z\longrightarrow1,
\end{equation}
because \(\pi_2(S^1)=0\) and \(F\) is connected. The meridian \(\mu\)
meets each fiber transversally in a single point, so the map to \(\Z\)
in \eqref{eq:fibration} sends \(\mu\) to a generator.

\subsection{Heegaard Floer homology and \texorpdfstring{\(L\)}{L}-spaces}\label{sec:Lspace}

Heegaard Floer homology \cite{OS2004a} assigns to a closed oriented
\(3\)-manifold \(Y\) a finite-dimensional vector space \(\HFhat(Y)\) over
\(\F_2\) (we use \(\F_2\) coefficients throughout), invariant up to
homeomorphism. If \(Y\) is a rational homology sphere, then
\(\dim_{\F_2}\HFhat(Y)\geq|H_1(Y;\Z)|\): the group splits as a direct
sum indexed by the spin\(^c\) structures of \(Y\), of which there are
\(|H^2(Y;\Z)|=|H_1(Y;\Z)|\), and each summand has Euler characteristic
\(\pm1\) \cite[Proposition~5.1]{OS2004b}. We call \(Y\) an
\emph{\(L\)-space} if equality holds. (The original definition
\cite[Definition~1.1]{OS2005} requires \(\HFhat(Y;\Z)\) to be a free
abelian group of rank \(|H_1(Y;\Z)|\); the \(\F_2\)-version above is
the one commonly used in the Heegaard Floer literature, and it is the one
used in this note.)

Lens spaces, including \(S^3\), are \(L\)-spaces
\cite[Proposition~3.1]{OS2004b}, which explains the name. The group
\(\HFhat(-Y)\) is the dual of \(\HFhat(Y)\)
\cite[Proposition~2.5]{OS2004b}, so \(Y\) is an \(L\)-space if and only
if \(-Y\) is.

A knot \(K\subset S^3\) is an \emph{\(L\)-space knot} if \(\Surg{r}{K}\)
is an \(L\)-space for some \(r\in\Q\); by (S2) such an \(r\) is
automatically non-zero. We say that \(K\) admits a \emph{positive}
\(L\)-space surgery if this holds for some \(r>0\). By (S4) and the
invariance of the \(L\)-space condition under orientation reversal,
\(K\) is an \(L\)-space knot if and only if \(K\) or its mirror image
admits a positive \(L\)-space surgery. The unknot is an \(L\)-space knot
by (S5), and so is every torus knot, since \((wt\pm1)\)-surgery on
\(T_{w,t}\) is a lens space \cite{Moser1971}.

\subsection{Group-theoretic tools}\label{sec:groups}

For a finitely generated group \(G\), let \(\rk(G)\) denote the minimal
number of generators of \(G\), and let \(G'=[G,G]\) denote its commutator
subgroup. If \(G\to Q\) is an epimorphism, then \(\rk(Q)\leq\rk(G)\).
Grushko's theorem \cite{Grushko1940} states that for finitely generated
groups \(A\) and \(B\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:grushko}
 \rk(A*B)=\rk(A)+\rk(B).
\end{equation}
We use the following consequence of the Poincar\'e conjecture, proved
by Perelman (see \cite{MorganTian2007} for a detailed exposition).

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perfect}
Let \(\Sigma\) be an integer homology sphere with \(\Sigma\not\cong S^3\).
Then \(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is a non-trivial perfect group, and
\(\rk(\pi_1(\Sigma))\geq2\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) were trivial, then \(\Sigma\) would be a simply
connected closed \(3\)-manifold, hence homeomorphic to \(S^3\) by the
Poincar\'e conjecture. Its abelianization is
\(H_1(\Sigma;\Z)=0\), so \(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is perfect. A non-trivial
cyclic group has non-trivial abelianization, so \(\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is not
cyclic, that is, \(\rk(\pi_1(\Sigma))\geq2\).
\end{proof}

A group \(G\) is \emph{normally generated} by a subset \(S\) if the
normal closure \(\langle\!\langle S\rangle\!\rangle\) is all of \(G\); the
\emph{weight} of \(G\) is the minimal size of such an \(S\). If \(G\) is
normally generated by one element and \(G\to Q\) is an epimorphism, then
\(Q\) is normally generated by the image of that element. By (S3), the
fundamental group of every Dehn surgery on a knot in \(S^3\) is normally
generated by the image of a meridian, that is, has weight at most one.
The group-theoretic input that limits the number of summands with
non-zero homology is the following theorem of Howie, previously known as
the Scott--Wiegold conjecture.

\begin{theorem}[Howie {\cite{Howie2002}}]\label{thm:howie}
Let \(a,b,c\geq2\). The free product
\((\Z/a\Z)*(\Z/b\Z)*(\Z/c\Z)\) is not normally generated by a single
element.
\end{theorem}

\section{The group-rank obstruction}\label{sec:rank}

In this section \(K\subset S^3\) is a fibered knot of genus \(g\), with
exterior \(E_K\) and fiber \(F\) as in Section~\ref{sec:fibered}. No
Floer-theoretic hypothesis is used here.

\begin{lemma}[Upper bound from the fiber]\label{lem:fiber}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be a fibered knot of genus \(g\), and let
\(M=\Surg{r}{K}\) for any slope \(r\in\Q\cup\{\infty\}\). Then
\[
 \rk\bigl(\pi_1(M)'\bigr)\leq 2g.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(\Pi=\pi_1(E_K)\) and \(G=\pi_1(M)\). We first identify \(\Pi'\)
with the fiber group. Let \(\phi\colon\Pi\to\Z\) be the map in
\eqref{eq:fibration}, so that \(\ker\phi=\pi_1(F)\cong F_{2g}\). Since
\(\Z\) is abelian, \(\phi\) factors as \(\phi=\psi\circ\alpha\), where
\(\alpha\colon\Pi\to\Pi/\Pi'=H_1(E_K;\Z)\cong\Z\) is the abelianization
and \(\psi\colon\Z\to\Z\) is a homomorphism. Both \(\alpha\) and
\(\phi\) send the meridian \(\mu\) to a generator (by (S2) and
Section~\ref{sec:fibered}, respectively), so \(\psi\) is onto, hence
\(\psi=\pm\mathrm{id}\) and \(\ker\phi=\ker\alpha=\Pi'\). Thus
\(\Pi'=\pi_1(F)\cong F_{2g}\).

By (S3), Dehn filling induces an epimorphism \(f\colon\Pi\to G\). For
any epimorphism of groups, \(f(\Pi')=G'\): the inclusion
\(f(\Pi')\subseteq G'\) is clear, and conversely every commutator
\([x,y]\) in \(G\) equals \(f([\tilde x,\tilde y])\) for lifts
\(\tilde x,\tilde y\) of \(x,y\). Hence \(G'\) is a quotient of
\(F_{2g}\), and \(\rk(G')\leq2g\).
\end{proof}

The next lemma is the heart of the argument. The idea is that
\(\pi_1(M)'\) is the fundamental group of the universal abelian cover of
\(M\), and that in this cover a homology sphere summand of \(M\) is
replicated once for each sheet, each replica contributing at least two
generators.

\begin{lemma}[Lower bound from the universal abelian cover]\label{lem:cover}
Let \(M\) be a closed connected oriented \(3\)-manifold with
\(H_1(M;\Z)\cong\Z/n\Z\) for some \(n\geq1\), and suppose that
\[
 M\cong X\#\Sigma,
 \qquad H_1(\Sigma;\Z)=0,\qquad \Sigma\not\cong S^3,
\]
for some closed oriented \(3\)-manifold \(X\). Then
\[
 \rk\bigl(\pi_1(M)'\bigr)\geq 2n.
\]
In particular, if \(M=\Surg{p/q}{K}\) with \(p\neq0\) for a fibered knot
\(K\) of genus \(g\), then a summand \(\Sigma\) as above can occur only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:numerator}
 |p|\leq g.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose closed balls \(B_X\subset X\) and \(B_\Sigma\subset\Sigma\) and
write \(M=X^\circ\cup_S\Sigma^\circ\), where
\(X^\circ=X\setminus\Int B_X\) and \(\Sigma^\circ=\Sigma\setminus\Int B_\Sigma\)
are the summands with the interior of a ball removed and \(S\) is the
common boundary \(2\)-sphere. By \eqref{eq:vk},
\(H_1(M;\Z)\cong H_1(X;\Z)\oplus H_1(\Sigma;\Z)=H_1(X;\Z)\), so
\(H_1(X;\Z)\cong\Z/n\Z\) and the inclusion \(X^\circ\hookrightarrow M\)
induces an isomorphism \(H_1(X^\circ;\Z)\to H_1(M;\Z)\).

Let \(G=\pi_1(M)\) and let \(\rho\colon\widetilde M\to M\) be the
connected covering space corresponding to the normal subgroup \(G'\)
(the \emph{universal abelian cover} of \(M\)). It is a regular covering
with deck group \(G/G'\cong H_1(M;\Z)\cong\Z/n\Z\),
so it has \(n\) sheets, and \(\pi_1(\widetilde M)\cong G'\). We use the
following standard fact about a regular covering with deck group \(Q\)
and a connected codimension-zero submanifold \(A\subseteq M\)
\cite[\S1.3]{HatcherAT}: if \(Q_A\) is the image of the composite
\(\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(M)\to Q\), then \(\rho^{-1}(A)\) has exactly
\([Q:Q_A]\) components, and each component is the connected covering of
\(A\) associated with the kernel of that composite.

We apply this to the two pieces of \(M\). For \(A=X^\circ\), the composite
\(\pi_1(X^\circ)\to G\to G/G'\cong H_1(M;\Z)\) is the abelianization of
\(\pi_1(X^\circ)\) followed by the isomorphism
\(H_1(X^\circ;\Z)\to H_1(M;\Z)\) noted above. So it is onto, and its kernel
is \(\pi_1(X^\circ)'=\pi_1(X)'\). Hence \(\rho^{-1}(X^\circ)\) is
connected, and it is the covering of \(X^\circ\) associated with
\(\pi_1(X)'\). If \(\widetilde X\to X\) denotes the connected
\(n\)-sheeted covering associated with \(\pi_1(X)'\), this says that
\[
 \rho^{-1}(X^\circ)\cong\widetilde X^\circ:=\widetilde X\setminus
 (\text{the \(n\) lifts of }\Int B_X).
\]
For \(A=\Sigma^\circ\), the group \(\pi_1(\Sigma^\circ)=\pi_1(\Sigma)\) is
perfect by Lemma~\ref{lem:perfect}, so it maps trivially to the abelian
deck group \(G/G'\). Hence \(\rho^{-1}(\Sigma^\circ)\) consists of \(n\)
components, each mapped homeomorphically onto \(\Sigma^\circ\).

The \(n\) boundary spheres of \(\widetilde X^\circ\) are the lifts of
\(S\), and each of them is glued to one copy of \(\Sigma^\circ\). Since
\(\widetilde X^\circ\) is connected, this exhibits
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cover-sum}
 \widetilde M\cong
 \widetilde X\#\underbrace{\Sigma\#\cdots\#\Sigma}_{n\text{ copies}}.
\end{equation}
All fundamental groups in sight are finitely generated, being
fundamental groups of compact manifolds. By \eqref{eq:vk}, Grushko's
theorem \eqref{eq:grushko} and Lemma~\ref{lem:perfect},
\[
 \rk(G')=\rk\bigl(\pi_1(\widetilde M)\bigr)
 =\rk\bigl(\pi_1(\widetilde X)\bigr)+n\,\rk\bigl(\pi_1(\Sigma)\bigr)
 \geq 2n.
\]

Finally, let \(M=\Surg{p/q}{K}\) with \(p\neq0\) and \(K\) fibered of
genus \(g\). By (S2), \(H_1(M;\Z)\cong\Z/|p|\Z\), so the first part applies
with \(n=|p|\) and gives \(\rk(G')\geq2|p|\), while
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber} gives \(\rk(G')\leq2g\). Hence \(|p|\leq g\).
\end{proof}

Howie's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:howie}) limits the summands with
non-zero homology; this is what produces the homology sphere summand to
which Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} applies.

\begin{lemma}[Consequence of Howie's theorem {\cite{Howie2002}}]\label{lem:howie}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be any knot and let \(p/q\) be a slope with
\(p\neq0\). Then at most two non-trivial prime summands of
\(\Surg{p/q}{K}\) have non-zero first integral homology.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set \(M=\Surg{p/q}{K}\) and let \(M_1\#\cdots\#M_k\) be its decomposition
into non-trivial prime summands. By \eqref{eq:vk} and (S2),
\[
 \bigoplus_{i=1}^k H_1(M_i;\Z)\cong H_1(M;\Z)\cong\Z/|p|\Z,
\]
so each \(H_1(M_i;\Z)\) is a direct summand of a finite cyclic group and
hence is finite cyclic. Suppose that three of them are non-zero, of
orders \(a,b,c\geq2\). By \eqref{eq:vk},
\(\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(M_1)*\cdots*\pi_1(M_k)\). Abelianizing those three
free factors and killing all the others defines an epimorphism
\[
 \pi_1(M)\twoheadrightarrow(\Z/a\Z)*(\Z/b\Z)*(\Z/c\Z).
\]
By (S3), \(\pi_1(M)\) is normally generated by one element, and this
property passes to the quotient (Section~\ref{sec:groups}). This
contradicts Theorem~\ref{thm:howie}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:large}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be a fibered knot of genus \(g\geq1\). If
\(p\neq0\) and \(|p|\geq2g-1\), then \(\Surg{p/q}{K}\) has at most two
non-trivial prime summands.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(M=\Surg{p/q}{K}\cong M_1\#\cdots\#M_k\)
with \(k\geq3\) and each \(M_i\) a prime manifold other than \(S^3\). By
Lemma~\ref{lem:howie}, at most two of the \(M_i\) have non-zero first
homology, so after renumbering \(H_1(M_k;\Z)=0\); thus \(M_k\) is an
integer homology sphere (Section~\ref{sec:prime}) with
\(M_k\not\cong S^3\). Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} with
\(X=M_1\#\cdots\#M_{k-1}\) and \(\Sigma=M_k\): since \(p\neq0\), it gives
\(|p|\leq g\), and together with the hypothesis,
\[
 2g-1\leq|p|\leq g .
\]
This forces \(g\leq1\), so \(g=1\) and \(|p|=1\).

It remains to rule out this endpoint. If \(|p|=1\), then
\(H_1(M;\Z)=0\) by (S2), so by \eqref{eq:vk} every \(M_i\) is an integer
homology sphere other than \(S^3\). Put \(G=\pi_1(M)\). Then \(G\) is
perfect, so \(G'=G\), and \eqref{eq:vk}, Grushko's theorem
\eqref{eq:grushko} and Lemma~\ref{lem:perfect} give
\[
 \rk(G')=\rk(G)=\sum_{i=1}^k\rk\bigl(\pi_1(M_i)\bigr)\geq2k\geq6.
\]
But Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber} gives \(\rk(G')\leq2g=2\), a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Proposition~\ref{prop:large} is Theorem~\ref{thm:fibered}. Note that it
makes no assumption on the knot beyond fiberedness. The proof actually
excludes a homology sphere summand whenever \(|p|>g\), by
\eqref{eq:numerator}. The threshold \(|p|\geq 2g-1\) in the statement is
the one that the Hom--Lidman--Zufelt theorem will supply for hyperbolic
\(L\)-space knots; for \(g=1\) it admits the value \(|p|=1\), which is
why the endpoint required the separate argument above.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:algebraic}
Lemma~\ref{lem:cover} has a purely group-theoretic core: if \(G=A*H\)
with \(H\) perfect and \(A/A'\cong\Z/n\Z\), then
\(G'\cong A'*H*\cdots*H\) with \(n\) copies of \(H\). This can also be
derived from the Kurosh subgroup theorem \cite{Kurosh1934}; the covering
space argument above makes the multiplicity \(n\) visible directly.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}\label{ex:torus}
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber} is sharp: for a torus knot, the cabling surgery
already exhausts the bound \(\rk(G')\leq2g\) with a free group, leaving
no room for a homology sphere summand. Let \(T_{a,b}\) be a torus knot
with \(a,b\geq2\) coprime, so that \(2g(T_{a,b})=(a-1)(b-1)\), and recall
that \(\Surg{ab}{T_{a,b}}\cong L(a,b)\#L(b,a)\) by Moser's theorem
\cite{Moser1971}. The fundamental group is \(G=(\Z/a\Z)*(\Z/b\Z)\), and
the kernel \(G'\) of its abelianization onto \(\Z/ab\Z\) is a free group
of rank \((a-1)(b-1)=2g\): indeed, in the \(ab\)-fold universal abelian
cover the punctured \(L(a,b)\) lifts to \(b\) copies of \(S^3\) with
\(a\) balls removed, the punctured \(L(b,a)\) lifts to \(a\) copies of
\(S^3\) with \(b\) balls removed, and these are glued along the \(ab\)
lifts of the separating sphere; the resulting manifold is a connected
sum of \(ab-(a+b)+1=(a-1)(b-1)\) copies of \(S^1\times S^2\). This is
consistent with \eqref{eq:numerator}, since \(ab>g\).
\end{example}

\section{Inputs from Heegaard Floer theory and Dehn surgery}\label{sec:inputs}

We now state the published theorems used in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. None of them is reproved here.

\begin{theorem}[Ni {\cite[Corollary~1.3]{Ni2007}}]\label{thm:ni}
Every \(L\)-space knot in \(S^3\) is fibered.
\end{theorem}

Ni's corollary explicitly allows a rational \(L\)-space surgery slope,
and its proof uses the structure theorem of Ozsv\'ath and Szab\'o
\cite{OS2005} for the knot Floer homology (the knot-level refinement of
\(\HFhat\)) of \(L\)-space knots; see also
Ni's erratum \cite{NiCorrigendum}, which repairs part of the proof of
the fiberedness detection theorem without affecting the statement, and
Ghiggini \cite{Ghiggini2008} for the genus-one case.

\begin{theorem}[Hom--Lidman--Zufelt {\cite[Theorem~1.3]{HLZ2015}}]\label{thm:hlz}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be a hyperbolic knot that admits a positive
\(L\)-space surgery. If \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is reducible, then
\(r=2g(K)-1\).
\end{theorem}

Two features of this statement matter for us. First, the reducible
surgery itself is not assumed to be an \(L\)-space; the theorem
constrains every reducible slope of \(K\). Second, the hyperbolicity
hypothesis cannot be dropped: the right-handed trefoil \(T_{2,3}\) has
genus \(1\) and admits a positive \(L\)-space surgery (its \(5\)- and
\(7\)-surgeries are lens spaces \cite{Moser1971}), but its reducible
surgery \(\Surg{6}{T_{2,3}}\cong L(2,3)\#L(3,2)\) has slope
\(6\neq 2g-1\).
This is why the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} treats non-hyperbolic
knots separately, using the following known cases of the Cabling
Conjecture.

\begin{theorem}[Moser {\cite{Moser1971}}, Scharlemann {\cite[Corollaries~4.4--4.5]{Scharlemann1990}}]\label{thm:cabling}
Let \(K\subset S^3\) be a non-trivial knot that is not hyperbolic, that
is, a torus knot or a satellite knot. If \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is reducible,
then \(K=C_{w,t}(J)\) is a cable, with \(w\geq2\) and \(\gcd(w,t)=1\), of
some knot \(J\), and \(r=wt\) is the cabling slope.
\end{theorem}

For torus knots this is Moser's classification of surgeries on
\(T_{w,t}=C_{w,t}(U)\): only the slope \(wt\) yields a reducible
manifold. For satellite knots it is Scharlemann's theorem; Corollary~4.4
of \cite{Scharlemann1990} treats a knot in a solid torus that is not
contained in a ball, and Corollary~4.5 applies it to satellite knots in
\(S^3\). Since composite knots are satellite knots
(Section~\ref{sec:types}), they are covered. The reduction of the
Cabling Conjecture to hyperbolic knots along these lines is standard and
is recorded, for instance, in the introduction of \cite{HLZ2015}.

\begin{theorem}[Gordon {\cite[Corollary~7.3]{Gordon1983}}]\label{thm:gordon}
Let \(J\subset S^3\) be a knot and let \(w\geq2\), \(t\) be coprime
integers. Then, up to the orientation of the lens space,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cable}
 \Surg{wt}{C_{w,t}(J)}\cong L(w,t)\#\Surg{t/w}{J}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

Formula \eqref{eq:cable} is consistent with (S2): both sides have first
homology of order \(|wt|=w\cdot|t|\), since \(\gcd(w,t)=1\). Geometrically,
the cabling annulus together with two meridian discs of the filling
solid torus forms a separating sphere exhibiting the decomposition
\eqref{eq:cable}: on one side it cuts off a punctured \(\Surg{t/w}{J}\),
and on the other a punctured lens space of order \(w\), obtained from
the solid torus \(\nbd J\) by attaching a \(2\)-handle along a curve of
winding number \(w\). This sphere is a reducing sphere when both factors
are non-trivial, but not always: for \(J\) the unknot and \(|t|=1\) the
cable \(C_{w,t}(J)\) is itself the unknot and \(\Surg{t/w}{J}\cong S^3\),
so the sphere bounds a ball.
%% FLAG: The attribution review could not access Gordon's original text
%% for Corollary 7.3; the formula and locator were corroborated through
%% explicit citations in later papers (Motegi--Teragaito), with the
%% opposite index order.

\begin{theorem}[Gordon--Luecke {\cite{GordonLuecke1987}}]\label{thm:gl}
If \(J\subset S^3\) is a non-trivial knot and \(r\in\Q\) is not an
integer, then \(\Surg{r}{J}\) is irreducible.
\end{theorem}

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}}\label{sec:proof}

Let \(K\subset S^3\) be an \(L\)-space knot and \(r\in\Q\cup\{\infty\}\).
We must show that \(\Surg{r}{K}\) has at most two non-trivial prime
summands.

\paragraph{Step 1: reduction to a positive \(L\)-space surgery.}
By the last paragraph of Section~\ref{sec:Lspace}, either \(K\) or its
mirror image \(\overline K\) admits a positive \(L\)-space surgery. By (S4),
\(\Surg{-r}{\overline K}\cong-\Surg{r}{K}\), and by
Section~\ref{sec:prime} a manifold and its orientation reversal have the
same number of non-trivial prime summands. Mirroring also preserves the
genus and the type (torus, satellite or hyperbolic) of a knot. Replacing
\((K,r)\) by \((\overline K,-r)\) if necessary, we may therefore assume
that \(K\) admits a positive \(L\)-space surgery.

\paragraph{Step 2: the unknot.}
If \(K\) is the unknot, then by (S5) \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is a lens space,
\(S^3\) or \(S^1\times S^2\). Lens spaces are irreducible and
\(S^1\times S^2\) is prime (Section~\ref{sec:prime}), so there is at most
one non-trivial prime summand. Henceforth \(K\) is non-trivial; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:ni} it is fibered, of genus \(g\geq1\).

\paragraph{Step 3: the slopes \(\infty\) and \(0\).}
By (S1), \(\Surg{\infty}{K}=S^3\) has no non-trivial prime summand. For
the slope \(0\), the filling solid torus has meridian \(\lambda=\partial F\),
where \(F\) is a fiber; the fibration of \(E_K\) restricts on
\(\partial E_K\) to the product fibration by longitudes, so the solid
torus is a union of discs capping off the fibers, and \(\Surg{0}{K}\) is a
bundle over \(S^1\) with fiber the closed surface \(\widehat F=F\cup D^2\)
of genus \(g\geq1\). The universal cover of \(\widehat F\) is \(\R^2\),
so the pull-back of the bundle to the universal cover \(\R\) of \(S^1\)
is \(\widehat F\times\R\), and the universal cover of \(\Surg{0}{K}\) is
\(\R^3\). Hence \(\Surg{0}{K}\) is irreducible (Section~\ref{sec:prime};
\cite[Proposition~1.6]{Hatcher3M}), so it is prime and has exactly one
non-trivial prime summand (it is not \(S^3\), having \(H_1\cong\Z\)).

\paragraph{Step 4: finite non-zero slopes.}
Let \(r=p/q\) with \(p\neq0\). If \(\Surg{r}{K}\) is prime, it has at most
one non-trivial prime summand. Otherwise it is reducible, and we
distinguish the type of \(K\) (Section~\ref{sec:types}).

\emph{Case 4a: \(K\) is hyperbolic.} By Step~1, \(K\) admits a positive
\(L\)-space surgery, so Theorem~\ref{thm:hlz} gives \(r=2g-1\), that is,
\(p=2g-1\geq1\) and \(q=1\). Since \(K\) is fibered of genus \(g\geq1\),
Proposition~\ref{prop:large} applies and shows that \(\Surg{r}{K}\) has at
most two non-trivial prime summands.

\emph{Case 4b: \(K\) is a torus knot or a satellite knot.} By
Theorem~\ref{thm:cabling}, \(K=C_{w,t}(J)\) with \(w\geq2\),
\(\gcd(w,t)=1\), and \(r=wt\). By Theorem~\ref{thm:gordon},
\(\Surg{r}{K}\cong L(w,t)\#\Surg{t/w}{J}\). The first factor is a lens
space with \(|H_1|=w\geq2\), hence a single non-trivial prime summand.
The slope \(t/w\) is not an integer, because \(w\geq2\) and
\(\gcd(w,t)=1\). If \(J\) is non-trivial, \(\Surg{t/w}{J}\) is irreducible
by Theorem~\ref{thm:gl}, hence prime, and contributes at most one
non-trivial prime summand. If \(J\) is the unknot, then \(t\neq0\) (as
\(\gcd(w,0)=w\geq2\)), so by (S5) \(\Surg{t/w}{J}\) is a lens space or
\(S^3\), and again contributes at most one. By uniqueness of the prime
decomposition, \(\Surg{r}{K}\) has at most two non-trivial prime
summands.

This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. \qed

\section{Comments}\label{sec:comments}

\begin{remark}[Where the \(L\)-space hypothesis is used]
The proof uses the \(L\)-space hypothesis only through
Theorems~\ref{thm:ni} and~\ref{thm:hlz}, in Steps~2 and~4a (Step~1
merely arranges the sign of the \(L\)-space slope that
Theorem~\ref{thm:hlz} requires). Consequently the same argument proves
the following statement, of which Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is a special
case: if \(K\) is a non-trivial fibered knot that is either
non-hyperbolic, or hyperbolic with every reducible slope \(p/q\)
satisfying \(|p|\geq2g(K)-1\), then every surgery on \(K\) has at most
two non-trivial prime summands. (Fiberedness is used in Step~3 for the
slope \(0\) and in Step~4a through Proposition~\ref{prop:large}.)
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[What is not proved]\label{rem:notproved}
The argument does not establish the Cabling Conjecture for hyperbolic
\(L\)-space knots. In Case~4a it handles a hypothetical reducible surgery
at slope \(2g-1\) directly, by excluding the integer homology sphere
summand that a third summand would force, without attempting to identify
that summand by Heegaard Floer methods. It does not exclude a reducible
surgery \(\Surg{2g-1}{K}\) on a hyperbolic \(L\)-space knot with exactly
two non-trivial prime summands, both with non-zero first homology.
For an arbitrary knot in \(S^3\), a surgery has at most three
non-trivial prime summands, and three summands would have to be two lens
spaces of coprime orders and an integer homology sphere; this combines
results of Sayari, Valdez-S\'anchez and Howie, see the introduction of
\cite{Howie2010}. Proposition~\ref{prop:large} excludes the last
configuration in the range \(|p|\geq2g-1\) for fibered knots without
using this classification.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The ambient manifold]
The hypothesis that \(K\) lies in \(S^3\) is used throughout: in (S2) and
(S3), in Ni's and Hom--Lidman--Zufelt's theorems, and in the Cabling
Conjecture. For knots in other \(L\)-spaces, a surgery can have three
non-trivial prime summands: a regular fiber of the Seifert fibration of
the Poincar\'e homology sphere (itself an \(L\)-space) has a surgery
homeomorphic to \(L(2,1)\#L(3,2)\#L(5,4)\) \cite{Caudell2021}.
\end{remark}
